benefits: Know exactly how high the sun is for any moment and place.
Essential for sizing solar panels and planning panel tilt.
Photographers can time golden hour and blue hour precisely.
Prayer-time and shadow-length calculations start from the zenith angle.

faqs.a: The zenith angle is measured from the point directly overhead (the zenith) down to the sun. Elevation is measured from the horizon up to the sun. They always add to 90 degrees: a zenith angle of 28 degrees means a solar elevation of 62 degrees.
faqs.q: What is the difference between zenith angle and solar elevation?

faqs.a: At the equator on an equinox at solar noon, the sun is directly overhead: zenith angle 0°, elevation 90°. More generally at solar noon the zenith angle equals the absolute difference between your latitude and the sun's declination.
faqs.q: When is the zenith angle zero?

faqs.a: Yes, at the poles. In polar summer the sun circles the sky without setting (midnight sun); in polar winter it never rises. The calculator handles this: elevation stays positive or negative for the whole day.
faqs.q: Can the sun stay up all day?

faqs.a: The NOAA solar equations used here are accurate to about ±0.01° for the years 2000–6000, ignoring atmospheric refraction. Near the horizon, refraction lifts the sun's apparent position by about 0.57°, which this calculator does not correct for.
faqs.q: How accurate is this calculation?

faqs.a: This calculator uses the mean solar position from date, time, and coordinates — pure astronomy, no weather data. Cloud cover, haze, and local obstructions are not modelled. For panel output estimates, combine the zenith angle with local irradiance data.
faqs.q: Does it account for clouds?

faqs.a: Solar noon is when the sun crosses your meridian (its highest point for the day), which rarely matches 12:00 on the clock because of your longitude, time zone, and the equation of time. This calculator finds it automatically — it is the moment the zenith angle is smallest.
faqs.q: What is solar noon and why is it not 12:00?

sun-position-calculator.formula:
cos(zenith) = sin(φ)·sin(δ) + cos(φ)·cos(δ)·cos(H)
φ = latitude, δ = solar declination, H = hour angle.
Solar elevation = 90° − zenith.
δ and H come from the NOAA solar equations (day of year, equation of time).
howTo: Pick the date and the local time you care about.
Enter your time zone as a UTC offset (for example, 5.5 for India, 3 for Saudi Arabia).
Enter your latitude and longitude in decimal degrees.
Read the zenith angle, solar elevation, declination, and day/night state.
keyFacts: The solar zenith angle is measured from directly overhead down to the sun.
Zenith angle + solar elevation always equals 90 degrees.
At solar noon, zenith = |latitude − solar declination|.
Solar declination swings between +23.44° and −23.44° through the year.
The calculation uses the NOAA solar position equations — pure static math.
Twilight is classified by elevation: civil (−6°), nautical (−12°), astronomical (−18°).

limitations: Ignores atmospheric refraction, which lifts the sun ~0.57° near the horizon.
No weather, clouds, or terrain — it is pure astronomy.
A spherical Earth is assumed; the error is negligible for this purpose.

sun-position-calculator.quickAnswer: The solar zenith angle measures how far the sun is from directly overhead: 0° means the sun is at the zenith, 90° means it is on the horizon. On 21 June at 12:00 UTC in London (51.5° N), the zenith angle is about 28.1° — because at solar noon it equals |latitude − declination| = |51.5 − 23.44|. Enter any date, time, and coordinates to get the zenith angle, elevation, and twilight state.

sun-position-calculator.workedExample:
London (51.5° N, 0°), 21 June, 12:00 UTC:
1. Day of year 172 → solar declination δ ≈ +23.44°.
2. At solar noon the hour angle H ≈ 0°.

sunrise-sunset-calculator.formula:
NOAA solar algorithm (simplified):
1. Day of year N; longitude hour = longitude / 15
2. Approx time t = N + (6 - lngHour) / 24 for sunrise, N + (18 - lngHour) / 24 for sunset
3. Sun's mean anomaly M = 0.9856 x t - 3.289
4. True longitude L = M + 1.916·sin M + 0.020·sin 2M + 282.634
5. Right ascension RA from L; declination via sinDec = 0.39782·sin L
6. Hour angle: cosH = (cos 90.833° - sinDec·sinLat) / (cosDec·cosLat)
7. Local mean time T = H + RA - 0.06571·t - 6.622; UTC time = T - lngHour

take-home-pay-calculator.assumptionNote: Applies one flat effective tax rate to taxable income (gross minus pre-tax deductions), then subtracts other deductions. Real tax systems are progressive and vary by location. An estimate for planning only.
benefits: Replaces paycheck guesswork with a concrete number before you sign an offer.
Shows how much pre-tax deductions (like retirement savings) actually save you in tax.
Makes pay frequencies comparable - monthly vs biweekly is not the same paycheck.
Free, instant, and private.

faqs.a: Use your effective rate, not your marginal bracket: total tax paid divided by total income. If you paid $12,000 on $60,000, your effective rate is 20% - even if your top dollars were taxed at 22%. Your pay stub or last tax return shows the real number.
faqs.q: What tax rate should I enter?

faqs.a: Pre-tax deductions - 401(k) contributions, HSA contributions, some insurance premiums - come out before tax is calculated, so they shrink your taxable income. A $3,000 pre-tax deduction at an 18% rate saves you $540 in tax, on top of the $3,000 itself.
faqs.q: How do pre-tax deductions help?

faqs.a: Marginal rate is the tax on your next dollar; effective rate is your average across all dollars. Progressive systems tax the first dollars at low rates and only the top slice at your bracket rate. This calculator uses one effective rate, which is why it is an estimate.
faqs.q: Marginal vs effective tax rate?

faqs.a: Withholding is often slightly off - too much and you get a refund, too little and you owe. This calculator estimates your true liability; if your actual withholding differs a lot, adjust your W-4 (US) or the equivalent form in your country.
faqs.q: Why does my paycheck differ from this?

faqs.a: Roughly 20 to 30% of gross for a typical middle-income earner in the US, depending on state and benefits. Enter your real effective rate from last year's return for the honest number.
faqs.q: How much of my paycheck goes to taxes?

faqs.a: No. This shows gross-to-net on the tax and deduction side only. Overtime, bonuses, and commissions raise the gross - enter your expected total annual gross including them for the full picture.
faqs.q: Does this include overtime and bonuses?

take-home-pay-calculator.formula:
Taxable income = gross - pre-tax deductions.
Tax = taxable income x (effective rate / 100).
Net annual = gross - tax - other deductions.
Per paycheck = net annual / paychecks per year (12, 26, or 52).
howTo: Enter your gross annual salary before any deductions.
Enter your effective tax rate as a percentage (total tax / total income).
Enter pre-tax deductions like retirement or HSA contributions.
Enter other annual deductions like insurance premiums.
Pick your pay frequency and read your take-home per paycheck.
keyFacts: Take-home pay = gross pay minus taxes minus deductions.
Pre-tax deductions shrink taxable income, so they save you tax at your effective rate.
Effective tax rate = total tax / total income - use this, not your marginal bracket.
Monthly = 12 paychecks, biweekly = 26, weekly = 52.
A flat-rate estimate cannot capture progressive brackets exactly.

tap-tempo.assumptionNote: Tempo is measured from your taps only - it assumes you tap steadily on the beat. A pause longer than 2.5 seconds resets the measurement, and the metronome click is a simple synthesized tick, not a studio click track.
benefits: Find the exact tempo of any song in seconds - just tap along.
Spacebar tapping works too, so you can tap without looking at the screen.
Built-in metronome plays your tapped tempo back for practice.
Milliseconds-per-beat readout helps you set delays and DAW tempos precisely.

faqs.a: BPM (beats per minute) counts how many beats fit in one minute. 60 BPM is one beat per second, 120 BPM is two beats per second. Most pop songs sit between 90 and 130 BPM; ballads are slower, dance tracks faster.
faqs.q: What is BPM?

faqs.a: Tap on the beat - usually where you would clap or nod your head. Tap at least 4-6 times; more taps give a steadier average. The tool uses your last 8 intervals, so early wobbly taps stop affecting the result.
faqs.q: How do I tap accurately?

faqs.a: Tap the big button with your finger, or press the spacebar - both work. On desktop, the spacebar is easiest because you can keep your eyes on the music. Each press counts as one beat.
faqs.q: Can I tap with the keyboard?

faqs.a: Yes - toggle the metronome on and it clicks at your tapped tempo, with a flashing display on each beat. It is perfect for checking whether a tempo feels right before you commit to it.
faqs.q: Does it have a metronome?

faqs.a: 60,000 divided by the BPM: at 120 BPM each beat lasts 500 ms. Producers use this to set delay times - a quarter-note delay at 120 BPM is 500 ms, an eighth note is 250 ms.
faqs.q: How do I convert BPM to milliseconds?

faqs.a: No - and that is normal. Human tapping varies by a few BPM even for steady tappers. The tool averages your last 8 taps to smooth this out. If the number jumps wildly, slow down and tap more deliberately on the strongest beats.
faqs.q: Why does my BPM keep changing slightly?

tap-tempo.formula:
BPM = 60,000 / average tap interval (ms)
Milliseconds per beat = 60,000 / BPM
Example: taps every 500 ms: BPM = 60,000 / 500 = 120.
howTo: Tap the big button (or press the spacebar) in time with the music - on every beat.
Tap at least 4 times; 8 or more taps give the steadiest reading.
Read your BPM. Toggle the metronome to hear it played back.
Tap Reset to start a fresh measurement.
Use the ms-per-beat value to set delay times or DAW tempos.
keyFacts: BPM = beats per minute: 60 BPM is one beat per second, 120 BPM is two per second.
The tool averages your last 8 tap intervals for a stable reading.
A gap of more than 2.5 seconds between taps resets the measurement.
Milliseconds per beat = 60,000 / BPM: at 120 BPM, each beat is 500 ms.
Most pop songs fall between 90 and 130 BPM.
Tapping on the strongest beats (kick drum, downbeats) gives the steadiest result.

tap-tempo.quickAnswer: Tap the big button (or the spacebar) on every beat - after 4 taps you get a live BPM reading that steadies as you keep tapping. Four taps 500 ms apart measure exactly 120 BPM, since BPM = 60,000 / average interval. Toggle the metronome to hear your tempo played back with a flash on each beat, and use the ms-per-beat readout to set delay times in your DAW.
tap-tempo.tagline: Tap along with any song to measure its BPM - with metronome and ms-per-beat readout.
tap-tempo.workedExample:
Finding a song's tempo:
1. The song plays. You tap on each kick-drum hit: tap... tap... tap... tap...
2. Your tap times: 0, 512, 1005, 1518 ms. Intervals: 512, 493, 513 ms.
3. Average interval = (512 + 493 + 513) / 3 = 506 ms.
4. BPM = 60,000 / 506 = 118.6 BPM.
5. Keep tapping: after 8 taps the reading settles at 118.8 BPM.
6. ms per beat = 60,000 / 118.8 = 505 ms - set your delay to 505 ms for quarter notes.

target-heart-rate-calculator.assumptionNote: 220 - age estimates max HR; individual max varies. Not for heart patients without medical guidance.
benefits: Stops the 'am I working hard enough?' guessing.

faqs.a: 60-100 bpm is the normal range; trained athletes often sit at 40-60. Lower generally means a fitter heart - unless it comes with dizziness, which needs a doctor.
faqs.q: What is a good resting heart rate?

faqs.a: Plain % of max ignores fitness. Two 30-year-olds share max 190, but with resting 50 vs 80 their aerobic zones differ hugely. Karvonen's reserve accounts for that.
faqs.q: Why Karvonen instead of plain percentages of max?

faqs.a: The 60-70% 'fat burn' zone uses the highest fat percentage - but higher zones burn more total calories and thus more total fat. For fat loss, total calories matter more than the zone name.
faqs.q: Which zone burns the most fat?

faqs.a: A graded exercise test in a lab is the gold standard. A field test (hard 3-minute hill effort, take the peak) gets close. Never max out alone or without warm-up.
faqs.q: How do I find my true max HR?

faqs.a: Watches often use % of max, not Karvonen, and estimate max from age. If your resting HR is low, Karvonen zones (like these) fit you better.
faqs.q: My watch zones differ - which is right?

faqs.a: Lightly. Start with perceived effort (can you talk?) and add zones once you train regularly. Zones shine for structured training, not first-month fitness.
faqs.q: Should beginners use heart-rate zones?

target-heart-rate-calculator.formula:
Max HR = 220 - age
HRR = max HR - resting HR
Target = resting HR + HRR x intensity

Example: age 30, resting 60
Max = 220 - 30 = 190; HRR = 190 - 60 = 130
Aerobic 70-80%: 60 + 130 x 0.70 = 151 to 60 + 130 x 0.80 = 164 bpm
howTo: Enter your age.
Enter your resting heart rate (morning, at rest).
Your max HR, reserve, and all five zones appear instantly.
Pick the zone matching your workout goal.
Recheck yearly - max HR falls about 1 beat per year with age.
keyFacts: Max HR is about 220 - age (estimate; fitter people often exceed it).
Heart-rate reserve (HRR) = max HR - resting HR.
Karvonen: target = resting + HRR x intensity.
Zones: 50-60% warm-up, 60-70% fat burn, 70-80% aerobic, 80-90% anaerobic, 90-100% max.
Measure resting HR first thing in the morning, before coffee.
Beta-blockers and some medicines blunt heart rate - zones do not apply the same way.

limitations: 220 - age is an estimate; true max varies by about 10-15 bpm.
Wrist sensors lag and misread during intervals - chest straps are better.
Heat, dehydration, caffeine, and illness raise HR at the same effort.

7. Max 90-100%: 177 to 190 bpm.

tdee-calculator.assumptionNote: TDEE is an estimate; real burn varies with tracking error, muscle mass and day-to-day life. Recalculate every few kilograms of change and adjust from real weight trends.
benefits: Ends guesswork: your maintenance calories come from your body and your life, not an average.
Goal targets turn lose/maintain/gain into one concrete daily number.
Shows exactly how much your activity level changes the equation.
The weekly pace estimate keeps expectations realistic.

faqs.a: A 500 kcal daily deficit loses about 0.45 kg per week. Larger deficits work faster but cost more muscle and are harder to sustain. Most people do best at 300-500 kcal.
faqs.q: What calorie deficit is best for weight loss?

faqs.a: Roughly 1 kg of body fat holds about 7,700 kcal, so a 500 kcal daily deficit predicts about 0.45 kg per week. Real loss varies with water shifts and muscle changes.
faqs.q: How fast will I lose weight?

faqs.a: Add 250-300 kcal above maintenance with progressive strength training. Faster surpluses mostly add fat, not muscle.
faqs.q: How should I eat to gain muscle?

faqs.a: Yes, but pick one: eat at maintenance while training hard (slow body recomposition) or alternate short gaining and cutting phases. Doing both at full speed is not realistic.
faqs.q: Can I lose fat and gain muscle at once?

faqs.a: BMR falls with weight, activity often drops unconsciously, and water retention masks fat loss. Recalculate TDEE, track honestly for two weeks, and only then adjust.
faqs.q: Why did my weight loss stall?

faqs.a: No. The formula is validated for adults. Children and teenagers need pediatric equations and a clinician's guidance.
faqs.q: Does TDEE work for teenagers?

tdee-calculator.formula:
TDEE = BMR x activity factor.
BMR (Mifflin-St Jeor, male) = 10 x kg + 6.25 x cm - 5 x age + 5.
Activity factors: 1.2 sedentary, 1.375 light, 1.55 moderate, 1.725 active, 1.9 very active.
Goal target = TDEE - 500 (lose), TDEE (maintain), TDEE + 500 (gain).
howTo: Select Male or Female and pick metric (cm/kg) or imperial (ft/in, lb).
Enter your age, height and weight.
Choose the activity level that best describes your typical week.
Pick your goal: lose, maintain or gain weight.
Read your TDEE, your daily calorie target and your expected weekly pace.
keyFacts: TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) is all the calories you burn in 24 hours.
It has four parts: BMR (60-70%), food digestion (about 10%), exercise and daily movement.
Activity factors multiply BMR: 1.2 for sedentary up to 1.9 for very active.
A 500 kcal daily deficit or surplus moves weight about 0.45 kg per week.
Weight change is driven by average intake over weeks, not single days.
A 30-year-old man at 70 kg, 175 cm, moderately active, burns about 2,556 kcal per day.
tdee-calculator.keywords: tdee calculator, total daily energy expenditure, maintenance calories calculator, calorie deficit calculator
limitations: Activity levels are self-reported and usually overestimated.
Cannot see muscle mass, so it underestimates muscular people.
Food labels and portion estimates add 10-20% error to real intake.
An estimate for planning, not a medical prescription.

tdee-calculator.workedExample:
Male, 30 years, 70 kg, 175 cm, moderate activity, goal: lose weight:

2. TDEE = 1,649 x 1.55 = 2,555.95, about 2,556 kcal/day.
3. Lose goal: 2,556 - 500 = 2,056 kcal/day.
4. Expected pace: 500 x 7 / 7,700 = 0.45 kg lost per week.

benefits: A 30-second brain warm-up that sharpens pattern recognition and planning.

faqs.a: X always moves first — that is the standard rule everywhere, and this game follows it. Going first is a real advantage: with perfect play X can force at least a draw, while O can only force a draw if X makes a mistake.
faqs.q: Who goes first in Tic Tac Toe?

faqs.a: No. The hard mode uses the minimax algorithm, which evaluates every possible continuation of the game and picks a move that guarantees at least a draw. The best result a human can achieve against perfect play is a draw. If you want wins, switch to easy mode, where the computer picks randomly.
faqs.q: Can the hard computer be beaten?

faqs.a: When all 9 squares are filled and none of the 8 winning lines holds three identical marks, nobody can win, so the game is a draw. Draws are common between careful players — in fact, perfect play from both sides always draws.
faqs.q: Why did my game end in a draw?

faqs.a: Easy mode picks a completely random empty square on every turn. It does not block your threats or build its own lines, so it is genuinely beatable and good for kids or casual play.
faqs.q: How does the easy computer work?

faqs.a: Take the center square if it is free — it belongs to 4 winning lines, more than any corner (3) or edge (2). Always block an immediate threat (two enemy marks with an empty third square). Then build forks: two threats at once, which cannot both be blocked.
faqs.q: What is the best strategy to win?

faqs.a: Scores are kept while this page stays open. Reloading or closing the tab resets them to zero. Nothing is stored on any server — the game never sends your data anywhere.

tic-tac-toe.formula:
Win check — any of these 8 lines all holding the same mark wins:
Rows: (1,2,3), (4,5,6), (7,8,9) | Columns: (1,4,7), (2,5,8), (3,6,9) | Diagonals: (1,5,9), (3,5,7).
Hard AI (minimax): every reachable board is scored — +10 for an O win, -10 for an X win, 0 for a draw, adjusted by depth so faster wins rank higher. The AI chooses the move with the highest guaranteed score, so it never loses.
tic-tac-toe.formulaHeading: How the game decides a win
howTo: Pick your mode: Two Players (a friend on the same screen), Easy (a relaxed computer), or Hard (an unbeatable computer).
X always starts. Tap any empty square to place your mark.
Players alternate turns. Watch for the winning line to light up when someone gets three in a row.
Press New Round to play again — your score is kept. Press Reset Scores to start the tally from zero.
On hard mode, try to force a draw: take the center if it is free, and always block an immediate threat.
keyFacts: Tic Tac Toe is played on a 3x3 grid with two marks: X and O. X always makes the first move.
You win by placing three of your marks in a straight line — any row, any column, or either diagonal.
There are 8 possible winning lines on the board: 3 rows, 3 columns, and 2 diagonals.
If all 9 squares fill up with no winning line, the game ends in a draw.
Perfect play from both sides always ends in a draw — the game is mathematically solved.
The hard computer on this page uses the minimax algorithm, which examines every possible future board and can never be beaten.

tic-tac-toe.workedExample:
Moves: X plays square 1, O plays 5, X plays 2, O plays 9, X plays 3.
1. The top row now reads X, X, X in squares 1, 2, 3.
2. The win check tests line (1,2,3): all three hold X. X wins.
3. The hard AI avoids this trap: after X takes 1 and 2, minimax scores every reply, sees that only square 3 stops the forced loss, and blocks there — which is why hard mode never loses.

faqs.a: Tilt-shift is a photography effect that keeps one horizontal band of the photo sharp while blurring the areas above and below it. The shallow-focus look tricks the brain into seeing a miniature model instead of a real scene.
faqs.q: What is the tilt-shift effect?

faqs.a: The tool renders a blurred copy of the photo, draws the sharp original underneath, then overlays the blurred version on the top and bottom regions with a gradient mask. The middle band stays sharp.
faqs.q: How does this tool create the effect?

faqs.a: Put the focus band over the main subject — usually slightly below the vertical center for landscapes. A band of 20–40% of the image height looks most natural.
faqs.q: Where should I place the focus band?

faqs.a: Feather controls how gradually the blur fades into the sharp band. Low feather gives a hard edge like a real tilt-shift lens; high feather gives a dreamy gradual transition.
faqs.q: What does feather do?

faqs.a: Yes, but gently: small amounts add atmosphere. Too much blur washes out the top and bottom completely, which can look artificial.
faqs.q: Can I blur the whole background?

faqs.a: No. The image is processed with the canvas API inside your browser.

tilt-shift-effect.workedExample:
You upload a 1200 × 800 city photo and set focus = 60%, band = 30%, blur = 8 px, feather = 25%.

Focus line y = 60% × 800 = 480 px.
Band top = 480 − (30% × 800) ÷ 2 = 480 − 120 = 360 px.
Band bottom = 480 + 120 = 600 px.
Feather = 25% × 800 = 200 px of soft transition.

The 240 px band from y = 360 to y = 600 stays tack sharp while the sky above and street below melt into blur — the city reads as a tiny model.

faqs.a: Divide your gross pay by your total hours worked: total pay / (regular hours + overtime hours). Because overtime hours are paid at 1.5x, the effective hourly rate always lands above your base rate. For example, $950 for 45 hours gives an effective rate of $21.11 per hour.

faqs.a: Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must receive at least 1.5x their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a work week. Salaried exempt workers are generally not entitled to overtime. Rules vary by country and state, so check your local labour law.
faqs.q: Who is legally entitled to time-and-a-half?

faqs.a: Most employers set the threshold at 40 hours per week. Some places use daily overtime (8+ hours per day) or count holiday hours differently. This calculator lets you set your own regular-hours threshold, so you can match whatever your employer uses.
faqs.q: Is overtime always after 40 hours?

faqs.a: Yes for many salaried non-exempt workers in the US: the FLSA looks at actual hours worked, not how you are paid. Your regular rate is salary / hours worked, and overtime is 1.5x that rate. Check with your HR department if you are unsure about your classification.

dayOffset = floor(totalSeconds / 86400)

faqs.a: Time value of money: the idea that money available now is worth more than the same amount later, because it can earn interest. All loan math, including this payment formula, is built on that principle.
faqs.q: What does TVM mean?

faqs.a: Because interest compounds on the unpaid balance. On a long loan you pay interest on interest for years before the principal shrinks meaningfully. Paying extra principal early cuts total interest dramatically.
faqs.q: Why is total interest so high?

faqs.a: Borrow less, get a lower rate, or stretch the term. Stretching the term lowers the payment but raises total interest, so compare the total-paid row, not just the payment.
faqs.q: How do I lower my payment?

faqs.a: Slightly. More frequent payments reduce the balance faster, which trims total interest a little. The bigger factor is always the rate and the term.
faqs.q: Does payment frequency matter?

faqs.a: Then the payment is simply the amount divided by the number of payments. The calculator handles this automatically: with no interest there is no compounding to solve for.
faqs.q: What if the interest rate is 0%?

faqs.a: Yes. The same math values an annuity: enter your target as the present value and the expected return as the rate, and the payment tells you what to save each period to reach it, ignoring that savings usually compound forward rather than amortize backward.
faqs.q: Can I use this for a savings goal instead of a loan?

time-value-of-money-calculator.formula:
Payment = PV x i / (1 - (1 + i)^-n).
PV = present value (loan amount), i = periodic rate (annual rate / frequency), n = total payments (years x frequency).
Example: 500,000 at 8.5% monthly for 5 years: i = 0.007083, n = 60; payment = 500,000 x 0.007083 / (1 - 1.007083^-60) = 10,258.27.

howcalc.heading: How we calculate
howcalc.s1: Monthly rate r = annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100, and n = years × 12 payments.
howcalc.s2: EMI = P × r × (1+r)^n ÷ ((1+r)^n − 1). With 0% interest it is simply P ÷ n.
howcalc.s3: Total interest = (EMI × n) − principal. The extra-EMI tip is simulated month by month.

time-zone-converter.formula:
For a wall time (y, m, d, h, min) in source zone S:
1. guess = Date.UTC(y, m-1, d, h, min)
2. offset = minutes such that local(S) = UTC + offset, read from Intl for that instant
3. utcMs = Date.UTC(y, m-1, d, h, min) - offset x 60000
4. repeat steps 2–3 twice more (settles DST edge cases)
5. target wall time = format utcMs with Intl in zone T

difference = offset(T) - offset(S) at that instant

keyFacts: A timezone is not a fixed offset — most zones shift twice a year for daylight saving, so the date you convert on matters.
UTC never observes daylight saving; it is the reference every conversion passes through.
The difference between two zones can change through the year: New York is 9 h 30 m behind Kolkata in October but the gap to London swings between 4 and 5 hours.
Half-hour and 45-minute zones exist — India (+5:30), Nepal (+5:45), and parts of Australia (+9:30) are common examples.

faqs.a: A service charge is set by the restaurant and usually goes to the house, though many places share it with staff. A tip goes directly to your server. If a service charge is already on the bill, check local custom - in many places that replaces the tip.

faqs.a: Yes - use 0% for takeaway or counter service where tipping is not expected. For sit-down service, leaving nothing for decent service is considered poor form in tipping cultures like the US. When in doubt, 15% is the safe minimum there.

faqs.a: The quiescent (no-signal) DC operating point of the transistor, described by IC and VCE. A good Q-point sits in the active region with headroom for the signal swing.
faqs.q: What is the Q-point?

faqs.a: A forward-biased silicon base–emitter junction drops about 0.7 V, so the emitter sits 0.7 V below the base: VE = VB − 0.7 V.
faqs.q: Why subtract 0.7 V?

faqs.a: The emitter current splits into collector current plus a small base current (IE = IC + IB). Since IB = IC/β is tiny for β ≥ 50, IC ≈ IE is an excellent approximation.
faqs.q: Why is IC approximately equal to IE?

faqs.a: If VCE falls near zero, the collector–base junction forward-biases and the transistor saturates — it acts like a closed switch instead of a linear amplifier.
faqs.q: What does saturation mean here?

faqs.a: A divider whose current is much larger than the base current, so VB barely moves when β varies. The rule R2 ≤ β×RE/10 is the standard check.
faqs.q: What is a stiff voltage divider?

faqs.a: The magnitudes work the same, but polarities reverse (VEE negative, currents flow out). This tool presents the NPN convention — flip signs for PNP.
faqs.q: Can I use this for PNP transistors?

transistor-bias-calculator.formula:
VB = VCC × R2/(R1+R2)
VE = VB − 0.7 V
IE = VE/RE,  IC ≈ IE
VCE = VCC − IC×(RC+RE)
IC(sat) = VCC/(RC+RE)
Stable if R2 ≤ β×RE/10
howTo: Enter the supply voltage VCC.
Enter the divider resistors R1 (top) and R2 (bottom) in kΩ.
Enter the collector resistor RC and emitter resistor RE in kΩ.
Enter the transistor's current gain β (hFE) from its datasheet.
Read IC, VCE, the node voltages, saturation current, region, and stability check.
keyFacts: Voltage-divider bias is the most stable common biasing method: the divider fixes VB nearly independent of β.
The Q-point (quiescent point) is the DC operating point — IC and VCE with no input signal.
Approximation used: VBE = 0.7 V for silicon, and IC ≈ IE (ignoring the small base current).
Active region needs VCE above ~0.2 V; near zero the transistor saturates and stops amplifying linearly.
Stability rule of thumb: R2 ≤ β×RE/10 keeps the divider stiff against β variation between transistors.
IC(sat) = VCC/(RC+RE) is the maximum possible collector current — your Q-point IC must stay well below it.

labels.assumptionNoteText: Assumes NPN silicon at room temperature: VBE = 0.7 V and IC ≈ IE.
labels.betaHint: From the transistor datasheet; typical 100–300 for small-signal BJTs.
labels.dividerHint: R1 connects VCC to the base node; R2 connects the base node to ground.
labels.reHint: RE provides negative feedback that stabilizes the bias point.
labels.stableNo: Unstable — lower R2 or raise RE

Assumes an NPN silicon transistor at room temperature; germanium or PNP needs sign adjustments.

transistor-bias-calculator.quickAnswer: The base voltage is set by the R1–R2 divider: VB = VCC × R2/(R1+R2). Subtract the 0.7 V base–emitter drop to get VE, divide by RE for the emitter current (IC ≈ IE), then VCE = VCC − IC×(RC+RE). With 12 V, 47k/10k, RC 2.2k, RE 1k, β 100: IC ≈ 1.41 mA and VCE ≈ 7.50 V — solidly in the active region.
transistor-bias-calculator.tagline: Find the Q-point of a voltage-divider biased BJT: IC, VCE, VB, VE, and stability.
transistor-bias-calculator.workedExample:
VCC 12 V, R1 47 kΩ, R2 10 kΩ, RC 2.2 kΩ, RE 1 kΩ, β 100.
VB = 12 × 10/57 = 2.11 V
VE = 2.11 − 0.7 = 1.41 V
IC ≈ IE = 1.41/1 = 1.405 mA
VCE = 12 − 1.405 × 3.2 = 7.50 V
IC(sat) = 12/3.2 = 3.75 mA — operating current is well below it.
VCE > 0.2 V → active region. R2 = 10 kΩ ≤ β×RE/10 = 10 kΩ → stable bias.

benefits: Solves the whole triangle — area, all three angles, perimeter and type — from just three sides.

faqs.a: Three lengths form a triangle only if the sum of any two is greater than the third: a + b > c, a + c > b, b + c > a. If any check fails — for example sides 1, 2, 10 — no triangle exists.
faqs.q: How do I know if three sides make a valid triangle?

faqs.a: Use Heron's formula: with semiperimeter s = (a+b+c)/2, area = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)). It works for any triangle when you know all three sides.
faqs.q: How is the area calculated from three sides?

faqs.a: The law of cosines: for the angle opposite side a, cos(A) = (b² + c² − a²) / (2bc), then A = arccos of that value. Repeat for each angle.
faqs.q: How are the angles found?

faqs.a: The circumradius R = abc / (4 × area) is the radius of the circle passing through all three vertices. The inradius r = area / s is the radius of the circle touching all three sides from inside.
faqs.q: What are the circumradius and inradius?

faqs.a: By sides: equilateral (all equal), isosceles (two equal), scalene (none equal). By angles: right (one 90°), obtuse (one > 90°), acute (all < 90°). A triangle gets one label from each group.
faqs.q: What do the triangle classifications mean?

triangle-calculator.formula:
Semiperimeter: s = (a + b + c) / 2
Heron's formula: Area = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c))

Law of cosines (angle A opposite side a):
cos(A) = (b² + c² − a²) / (2bc)

Circumradius: R = abc / (4 × Area)
Inradius:     r = Area / s

Valid only if: a + b > c, a + c > b, b + c > a

faqs.a: ULID stands for Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier. It is a 26-character ID made of a 48-bit millisecond timestamp plus 80 bits of random data, encoded in Crockford Base32. Because the timestamp comes first, ULIDs sort in the order they were created.
faqs.q: What is a ULID?

faqs.a: Use ULID when you want IDs that sort by creation time, are shorter (26 vs 36 characters) and are URL-safe. Use UUID when you want the widest library support or must not expose creation time. Both are effectively collision-free.
faqs.q: ULID vs UUID: which should I use?

faqs.a: The random 16 characters are drawn from crypto.getRandomValues(), which is a cryptographically secure random source in every modern browser. They are suitable for IDs; they are not passwords or secret tokens, so treat them as public identifiers.
faqs.q: Are these ULIDs cryptographically secure?

faqs.a: Only if both the millisecond timestamp and all 80 random bits match, which has a probability of about 1 in 1.2 million billion billion for the same millisecond. In practice, collisions do not happen.
faqs.q: Can two ULIDs be identical?

faqs.a: ULIDs use Crockford Base32, which deliberately drops I, L, O and U because they are easy to confuse with 1, 1, 0 and V. This makes ULIDs safer to read aloud or copy by hand.
faqs.q: Why are the letters I, L, O and U missing?

faqs.a: Decode the first 10 characters as a Base32 number using the Crockford alphabet. The result is the Unix timestamp in milliseconds. This tool shows the decoded creation time next to every generated ULID.
faqs.q: How do I extract the timestamp from a ULID?

ulid-generator.workedExample:
The first 10 characters of a ULID encode the timestamp. Take "01ARZ3NDEK": in Crockford Base32, 0=0, 1=1, A=10, R=24, Z=31, 3=3, N=21, D=13, E=14, K=19. Multiply each value by the matching power of 32 and add them:
1 x 32^8 + 10 x 32^7 + 24 x 32^6 + 31 x 32^5 + 3 x 32^4 + 21 x 32^3 + 13 x 32^2 + 14 x 32 + 19 = 1469922850259
That is 1,469,922,850,259 milliseconds since the Unix epoch (30 July 2016). The remaining 16 characters carry the 80 bits of random data.
mistakes: Using ULIDs where timing must stay secret — the timestamp is baked into the ID. Anyone can read when a record was created.
Treating a ULID as a secret token or password — it proves nothing and authenticates nothing. It's an identifier, not a credential.
Showing sequential ULIDs to competitors — because they sort by creation time, rivals can estimate your growth rate from your order numbers.
Generating IDs on machines with wrong clocks — if the system time is off, the sort order breaks. Clock skew defeats the whole point.
Skipping the database uniqueness check — collisions are astronomically unlikely, but your database constraint is still the real guarantee.

faqs.a: Unicode assigns every character a number called a code point. The \uXXXX escape writes that number in four hexadecimal digits, so A (code point 65, hex 41) becomes \u0041.

faqs.a: Characters above U+FFFF (most emoji) do not fit in four hex digits, so they are stored as two UTF-16 surrogate halves, each written as its own \uXXXX escape. The pair decodes back to one character.
faqs.q: What are surrogate pairs?

faqs.a: The decoder only replaces well-formed \u followed by exactly four hex digits. Anything else — like \u12 or \uZZZZ — is left untouched in the output.
faqs.q: What happens to invalid escapes?

faqs.a: UTM parameters are five short query tags (utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_term, utm_content) that you add to a URL. Analytics tools read them to tell you exactly which link, email or ad brought each visitor.
faqs.q: What are UTM parameters?

faqs.a: All five exist, but only three are required for clean reports: utm_source (where the traffic comes from), utm_medium (the channel, e.g. email or cpc) and utm_campaign (the campaign name). utm_term and utm_content are optional extras.
faqs.q: Which UTM parameters are required?

faqs.a: Keep one naming convention and stick to it: lowercase, underscores instead of spaces, e.g. summer_sale. Mixing Summer-Sale, summer sale and SUMMER_SALE creates three separate rows in your reports.
faqs.q: How should I name my campaigns?

faqs.a: utm_source names the referrer (newsletter, facebook, google). utm_medium names the channel (email, social, cpc, referral). Example: source=newsletter, medium=email for a link in your email newsletter.
faqs.q: What is the difference between utm_source and utm_medium?

faqs.a: Yes. This tool preserves anything already in the URL: existing query parameters and the #fragment stay in place, and the UTM tags are added alongside them.
faqs.q: Can I add UTM tags to a URL that already has parameters?

faqs.a: No. UTM tags only label the visit for your own analytics; they do not change what the visitor sees, and they do not affect search rankings.
faqs.q: Do UTM parameters hurt SEO?

utm-builder.formula:
final URL = base URL + "?" + "utm_source=" + source + "&utm_medium=" + medium + "&utm_campaign=" + campaign [+ "&utm_term=" + term] [+ "&utm_content=" + content]
Values are percent-encoded. If the base URL already has a query string, new parameters are appended with "&".
howTo: Paste your destination page URL into the Website URL field.

Optionally add utm_term (paid keyword) and utm_content (to tell two links apart).
Copy the finished URL and use it in your email, ad or social post.
keyFacts: UTM stands for Urchin Tracking Module, from the Urchin analytics software Google acquired in 2005; the naming lives on in Google Analytics.
The five standard parameters are utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_term and utm_content.
utm_source identifies the referrer, utm_medium the marketing channel, and utm_campaign the specific promotion.
utm_term records the paid-search keyword, and utm_content distinguishes links that point to the same URL (e.g. two buttons in one email).
Analytics platforms read UTM tags automatically; visitors never see anything different on the page.
Special characters in values are percent-encoded, so spaces and symbols never break the link.

benefits: No coordination needed: any device can mint IDs independently without a central counter.

faqs.a: UUID stands for Universally Unique Identifier. It is a 128-bit value, usually written as 32 hexadecimal digits in five groups (8-4-4-4-12), standardized by RFC 4122 and used as unique keys in databases, APIs and distributed systems.
faqs.q: What is a UUID?

faqs.a: Version 4 UUIDs are generated from random data: 122 of the 128 bits are random, which gives about 5.3 x 10^36 possible values. Other versions derive from timestamps (v1), names (v3, v5) or sortable timestamps (v7).
faqs.q: What is a version 4 UUID?

faqs.a: The 13th hexadecimal digit is the version: for v4 it is always 4. The 17th digit encodes the variant: 8, 9, a or b, which means the first two bits are 10, the RFC 4122 variant. Check any UUID from this tool and you will see that pattern.
faqs.q: How can I tell it is really version 4?

faqs.a: The chance of a duplicate is about 1 in 5.3 x 10^36. You would need to generate billions of UUIDs per second for centuries before a collision became likely. For practical purposes, v4 UUIDs never collide.
faqs.q: Can two UUIDs be the same?

faqs.a: Use UUID when you need maximum compatibility and must not expose creation time. Use ULID when you want shorter IDs that sort by creation time and are friendlier in URLs. Both are free on this site.
faqs.q: UUID or ULID: which should I pick?

faqs.a: No. crypto.randomUUID() is a native browser API present in all modern browsers. No library, no network and no server is involved.
faqs.q: Does this tool use any external library?

uuid-generator.formula:
UUID v4 = 32 hex digits in 8-4-4-4-12 groups (36 chars with hyphens)
122 random bits + 4 version bits (0100) + 2 variant bits (10)
Possible values: 2^122 = approx. 5.3 x 10^36

keyFacts: A UUID is 128 bits long, written as 32 hexadecimal digits in the pattern 8-4-4-4-12, e.g. 6ec0bd7f-11c0-43da-975e-2a8ad9ebae0b.
Version 4 UUIDs are random: 122 of the 128 bits are random, 4 bits mark the version (0100) and 2 bits mark the RFC 4122 variant (10).
The 13th hex digit of a v4 UUID is always 4, and the 17th digit is always 8, 9, a or b.
UUIDs were standardized in RFC 4122 and are supported by every major database, language and platform.
Because they need no central authority, UUIDs work perfectly for offline-first apps and distributed systems.

uuid-generator.workedExample:
Take the UUID 6ec0bd7f-11c0-43da-975e-2a8ad9ebae0b.
Step 1: count the hex digits: 8 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 12 = 32 digits = 128 bits. Step 2: look at the 13th hex digit: the digits run 6,e,c,0,b,d,7,f (1-8), 1,1,c,0 (9-12), then 4 is the 13th digit, so the version is 4. Step 3: look at the 17th hex digit: digits 13-16 are 4,3,d,a, so the 17th is 9. Hex 9 = binary 1001, which starts with the variant bits 10, marking it RFC 4122. With 122 random bits, about 5.3 x 10^36 different v4 UUIDs exist.
mistakes: Using v4 UUIDs where order matters — they're random, so sorting them means nothing. Use ULID or UUID v7 if you need chronological IDs.
Treating a UUID as a password or secret — it's an identifier, not a credential. It authenticates nothing.
Pasting the braced format into a system that rejects it — some APIs accept only plain hex. Match the format to what the field expects.
Storing UUIDs in a column that's too short — 36 characters need room. A VARCHAR(32) silently truncates them and breaks everything.
Expecting to generate the same UUID twice — there's no seed and no pattern. Every batch is brand new, every time.

benefits: VA loans need no down payment and no private mortgage insurance - see the true cost in one place.

faqs.a: The VA funding fee is a one-time fee paid to the Department of Veterans Affairs that keeps the loan program running without taxpayer cost. For first-time use with zero down payment it is 2.15% of the loan (higher for subsequent use, lower with a down payment). Most borrowers finance it into the loan rather than paying cash at closing.
faqs.q: What is the VA funding fee?

faqs.a: Veterans receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability are exempt from the funding fee, as are some surviving spouses. If you are exempt, set the funding fee to 0% in this calculator.
faqs.q: Who is exempt from the funding fee?

faqs.a: The big ones: no down payment required, no private mortgage insurance, competitive interest rates, and limits on closing costs the veteran can pay. The trade-off is the funding fee and the requirement to use the home as your primary residence.
faqs.q: What are the main VA loan benefits?

faqs.a: Eligibility requires a Certificate of Eligibility (COE), generally available to veterans, active-duty service members, National Guard and Reserve members with qualifying service, and some surviving spouses. Your lender can usually pull the COE for you in minutes.
faqs.q: Who is eligible for a VA loan?

faqs.a: Yes, but the fee is higher: 3.3% with zero down for subsequent use (vs 2.15% first use). Making a down payment of 5% or more lowers it. If you plan to use the benefit again, this calculator's fee slider lets you compare both scenarios.
faqs.q: Can I use a VA loan more than once?

faqs.a: Usually yes - the fee is rolled into the loan balance at closing, so you pay interest on it over the life of the loan. You can also pay it in cash at closing if you prefer a smaller loan. This calculator assumes it is financed, which is the common choice.
faqs.q: Is the funding fee added to the loan?

va-mortgage-calculator.formula:
Base loan = home price - down payment.
Funding fee = base loan x fee% / 100.
Total loan = base loan + funding fee.
Monthly rate r = annual rate / 12; n = years x 12.
Monthly payment = total loan x r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n).
howTo: Enter the home price and any down payment (0 is normal for VA loans).
Set your VA funding fee percentage (2.15% first use with 0 down; 0% if exempt).
Enter the interest rate and loan term from your offer.
Read your monthly payment, the financed fee, and the total loan balance.
Compare fee scenarios to see the real cost of financing the fee vs paying it at closing.

howcalc.heading: How we calculate
howcalc.s1: Monthly rate r = annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100, and n = years × 12 payments.
howcalc.s2: EMI = P × r × (1+r)^n ÷ ((1+r)^n − 1). With 0% interest it is simply P ÷ n.
howcalc.s3: Total interest = (EMI × n) − principal. The extra-EMI tip is simulated month by month.

keyFacts: VA loans are backed by the US Department of Veterans Affairs and require no down payment.
No private mortgage insurance (PMI) on VA loans - a major saving vs conventional loans with small deposits.
The funding fee replaces PMI: 2.15% of the loan for first use with 0 down, 3.3% for subsequent use.
Veterans with a service-connected disability rating are exempt from the funding fee.
The fee drops with a down payment: around 1.5% with 5% down, 1.25% with 10% down.
You need a Certificate of Eligibility (COE); most lenders can obtain it for you quickly.

faqs.a: Value Added Tax (VAT) is a consumption tax added at each stage of production, but the consumer ultimately pays it. In the UK the standard rate is 20%; Saudi Arabia and the UAE charge 15% and 5% respectively; India uses GST (a similar system) with rates of 5%, 12%, 18%, and 28%.
faqs.q: What is VAT?

faqs.a: When you remove VAT, you divide by (1 + rate), not subtract the percentage. Removing 20% from £120: 120 / 1.2 = £100, not £96. Subtracting 20% from £120 gives the wrong answer (£96) because the original 20% was calculated on the £100 net price.
faqs.q: Why can't I just subtract 20% to remove VAT?

faqs.a: The UK VAT registration threshold is £90,000 of taxable turnover in a rolling 12-month period. Below that, registration is voluntary. Voluntary registration lets you reclaim VAT on expenses but forces you to charge VAT to customers - worth it mainly for B2B businesses.
faqs.q: When must a UK business register for VAT?

faqs.a: VAT is a European-style tax charged on value added at each stage; GST (Goods and Services Tax) is India's unified version of the same idea. Both are ultimately paid by the end consumer. The maths in this calculator works identically for both.
faqs.q: VAT vs GST - what is the difference?

faqs.a: Yes - many items have reduced or zero rates. In the UK: 5% on domestic energy, 0% on most food, books, and children's clothes. Saudi Arabia applies 15% broadly with limited exemptions. Check your country's tax authority for the exact rate on your item.
faqs.q: Is VAT always 20% / 15%?

vat-calculator.formula:
Adding VAT: gross = net x (1 + rate).
VAT amount = net x rate.
Removing VAT: net = gross / (1 + rate).
VAT amount = gross - net.
Example (20%): removing from 120 -> 120 / 1.2 = 100.

Set the VAT rate (20% is the UK standard, 15% Saudi, 5% UAE).

howcalc.heading: How we calculate
howcalc.s1: Tax = taxable amount × rate ÷ 100.
howcalc.s2: Add mode: total = price + tax. Strip mode: net = total ÷ (1 + rate ÷ 100).

keyFacts: UK standard VAT is 20%; reduced 5% on energy, 0% on most food, books, and children's clothes.
Saudi Arabia charges 15% VAT, the UAE 5%, India uses GST at 5/12/18/28%.
UK businesses must register for VAT at £90,000 taxable turnover in 12 months.
Removing VAT means dividing by 1.2 (at 20%), not subtracting 20% - a common and costly mistake.
Consumer prices in the UK and Gulf must legally be shown VAT-inclusive.

benefits: Confirm your phone's vibration motor still works.

faqs.a: The Vibration API is an Android/Chrome feature. iPhones do not expose vibration to web pages at all, so the page shows not supported. Desktops have no vibration motor, so they show the same message.
faqs.q: Why does it say not supported on my iPhone?

faqs.a: Press Stop, which sends vibrate(0) and cancels the pattern immediately. Patterns are short anyway - the longest preset here is about two seconds.
faqs.q: How do I stop a vibration pattern?

faqs.a: Yes, the SOS pattern is the classic distress signal: three short bursts, three long, three short. It is the same rhythm used in Morse code SOS. Use it to test that your motor can handle rapid on-off switching.
faqs.q: Is the SOS pattern a real distress signal?

faqs.a: No. The web API only accepts on/off timing - it cannot control strength, frequency, or waveform. All patterns are the motor's fixed buzz chopped into timed bursts.
faqs.q: Can this test vibration strength or intensity?

faqs.a: Try another browser (Chrome on Android is the reference), make sure the phone is not in a mode that disables haptics, and check the system vibration setting. Some phones have a master vibration switch that overrides apps and pages.
faqs.q: The page says supported but I feel nothing. Why?

vibration-test.formula:
A pattern is a list of timings in milliseconds.
Odd positions (1st, 3rd, 5th) = vibrate that long.
Even positions = pause that long.
Example: [200, 150, 200] = buzz 200ms, rest 150ms, buzz 200ms.
Total = 200 + 150 + 200 = 550ms.
howTo: Open this page on your phone and hold the phone in your hand.
Press one of the pattern buttons: short, long, double, or SOS.
Feel the buzz and confirm it matches the described pattern.
Try a custom duration: enter milliseconds and press Vibrate.
Press Stop to cancel any pattern immediately.
keyFacts: The Vibration API vibrates the phone's motor in timed on/off bursts.
Patterns are millisecond lists: odd entries vibrate, even entries pause.
SOS = three short, three long, three short - the classic distress rhythm.
iPhones do not expose vibration to web pages; desktops have no motor.
vibrate(0) stops any running pattern instantly.
Intensity cannot be controlled - only the timing of the fixed buzz.

voltage-drop-calculator.workedExample:
230 V, single phase, copper, 2.5 mm², 30 m, 16 A.
Vd = 2 × 0.0172 × 30 × 16 ÷ 2.5 = 16.512 ÷ 2.5 = 6.60 V
Drop % = 6.60 ÷ 230 × 100 = 2.87%
Voltage at load = 230 − 6.60 = 223.4 V
Max current for 5% = 0.05 × 230 × 2.5 ÷ (2 × 0.0172 × 30) = 27.9 A
Verdict: 2.87% is within the 5% power limit (but above the 3% lighting limit).

faqs.a: Aim to shrink the waist while keeping the hips stable: regular brisk walking, strength training, enough sleep, and less added sugar and alcohol all target belly fat. Even a 0.03 to 0.05 drop - about 3 to 5 cm off the waist - moves many people a full risk category.
faqs.q: How can I lower my waist-to-hip ratio?

faqs.a: Yes, modestly. Hip circumference reflects bone structure and gluteal muscle and fat, which change slowly. That is fine - a falling ratio driven by a shrinking waist is the meaningful kind of progress.
faqs.q: Does the hip measurement ever change?

faqs.a: No. Children's body proportions differ, and the adult WHO cut-offs do not apply. Paediatric growth charts use waist measurements against age, not this ratio.
faqs.q: Can children use this calculator?

waist-to-hip-ratio-calculator.formula:
WHR = waist circumference / hip circumference.
Both measurements must use the same unit.
WHO risk bands - men: below 0.90 low, 0.90-0.99 moderate, 1.00+ high.
Women: below 0.80 low, 0.80-0.84 moderate, 0.85+ high.
Example: 76 / 100 = 0.76 (low risk for a woman).

Measure your waist at its narrowest point, roughly at navel level, after breathing out.
Measure your hips at their widest point around the buttocks.

If you land in moderate or high risk, pick one habit - a daily 30-minute walk is a strong start - and recheck monthly.
keyFacts: WHR = waist circumference divided by hip circumference, both in the same unit.
WHO low-risk cut-offs: below 0.90 for men, below 0.85 for women.
Belly fat (visceral fat) raises heart and diabetes risk more than fat on the hips and thighs.
Research finds WHR predicts cardiovascular risk better than BMI in many studies.
Measure the waist at the narrowest point after breathing out, and the hips at the widest point.
A tape measure reading is a screening signal, not a diagnosis - trends matter more than one reading.

walking-time-calculator.assumptionNote: Pace categories and age ranges use published averages for comfortable walking speeds. Terrain, fitness, and stride length shift them in real life.
benefits: Gives you a realistic target for the classic one-mile walking test used by many fitness programmes.
Knowing your pace helps you plan routes - a 30-minute walk at 5 km/h covers about 1.55 miles.
Tracking your mile time over weeks shows fitness gains that a scale never will.
The age comparison tells you honestly where you stand, without judgment.

faqs.a: For most adults, 4.8 to 6.4 km/h (3 to 4 mph) is a solid moderate pace - that is roughly a 19 to 25 minute mile. Health guidelines count anything around 100 steps per minute as moderate intensity. If you can talk but not sing while walking, your pace is about right.
faqs.q: What is a good walking pace?

faqs.a: Most adults take 15 to 25 minutes. A brisk walker does it in about 15 to 17 minutes, an average walker in 19 to 22 minutes, and a relaxed walker in 25 minutes or more. Anything under 20 minutes is a good everyday pace.
faqs.q: How long should it take to walk a mile?

faqs.a: On average, yes - comfortable walking speed peaks around the 40s and declines gradually after 60, dropping more noticeably past 75. But the range within any age group is wide, and regular walking slows that decline considerably.
faqs.q: Is walking speed really slower with age?

faqs.a: Walk a known distance - most maps or a 400 m running track work - and time yourself with a phone stopwatch. Divide distance by time in hours. For example, 1 km in 12 minutes is 5 km/h.
faqs.q: How do I measure my walking speed without a tracker?

faqs.a: Speed is distance per time (km/h or mph) - higher means faster. Pace is time per distance (min/km or min/mi) - lower means faster. Runners and walkers usually talk in pace, so this tool shows you both.
faqs.q: What is the difference between pace and speed?

faqs.a: Yes, roughly in proportion to speed. A 70 kg person burns about 240 kcal per hour at 5 km/h and about 350 kcal per hour at 6.5 km/h. Covering the same mile faster also takes less time, so per-mile the difference is smaller than per-hour.
faqs.q: Does walking faster burn more calories?

walking-time-calculator.formula:
Metric: minutes = 1.609344 / speed(km/h) x 60.
Imperial: minutes = 60 / speed(mph).
Pace per km (min/km) = 60 / speed(km/h).
Pace per mile (min/mi) = 60 / speed(mph).
Example: at 5 km/h -> 1.609344 / 5 x 60 = 19.31 minutes = 19 min 19 s.
howTo: Pick your units: metric (km/h) or imperial (mph).
Enter your steady walking speed. Not sure? Walk a known distance, time it, and divide distance by time.
Enter your age so the tool can compare your pace with the typical range for your age group.
Read your mile time, your pace per kilometre or per mile, and your speed category instantly.
If your pace falls below the typical range, build up gradually - add five minutes to your daily walk each week.
keyFacts: One mile equals 1.609344 km. Your mile time in minutes is 60 divided by your speed in mph, or (1.609344 / speed in km/h) x 60.
A pace of 12:00 min/km equals 19:19 min/mi - the pace of a 5 km/h walker.

Brisk walking - roughly 6 km/h or about 100 steps per minute - is the intensity tied to most health benefits in research.
Treadmill speeds and outdoor speeds feel different: wind, hills, and surface all change your real pace.
Fitness trackers and phones usually measure distance well but can be off by 5 to 10% on pace, so time your walk if you want a precise number.

walking-time-calculator.workedExample:
Speed 5 km/h, age 30:

2. Convert to minutes: 0.32187 x 60 = 19.31 minutes, i.e. 19 min 19 s.

5. Pace per mile: 60 / 3.1069 = 19.31 min/mi (19:19).
6. Category: 5 km/h is moderate walking. The typical comfortable range for ages 30-39 is 4.8-5.1 km/h, so this pace sits right inside it.

weight-calculator.assumptionNote: Gravity values are average surface values. Your mass - the amount of matter in your body - stays the same everywhere; only your weight changes.
benefits: Makes the mass-vs-weight distinction click in a way textbooks rarely do.
Great for students: enter your mass once and tour the whole solar system instantly.
Removes unit confusion by showing newtons, kilogram-force, and pound-force side by side.
The custom gravity mode covers anything else - an elevator, an aircraft, or a sci-fi planet.

faqs.a: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms, and it is the same everywhere. Weight is the force gravity pulls that mass with, measured in newtons, and it changes with gravity. On the Moon you weigh less because the Moon pulls weaker - but your mass is identical.
faqs.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?

faqs.a: Your weight in kilograms - what bathroom scales display - is kilogram-force, an old unit equal to the force of Earth gravity on one kilogram. Physicists prefer newtons. On Earth the two numbers are nearly equal, which is why scales get away with it.
faqs.q: Why does my scale show kg if weight is in newtons?

faqs.a: Surface gravity of the Moon is about 1.62 m/s squared, roughly one-sixth of Earth's 9.807. A 70 kg person weighs about 686 N on Earth and only 113 N on the Moon - that is why Apollo astronauts could bounce around in heavy suits.
faqs.q: How much would I weigh on the Moon?

faqs.a: Divide your Earth weight in newtons by 9.807 to get your mass in kilograms. That mass never changes - multiply it by any gravity to get your weight there.
faqs.q: How do I find my mass from my weight?

faqs.a: Roughly 2.5 times your Earth weight: Jupiter's surface gravity is about 24.79 m/s squared. A 70 kg person would weigh about 1,736 N there - over 176 kilogram-force. You would not enjoy standing up.
faqs.q: How much would I weigh on Jupiter?

faqs.a: The International Space Station is in free fall around Earth, so astronauts and everything around them accelerate together - scales read zero. They are not beyond gravity; at that altitude gravity is still about 90% of Earth's surface value.
faqs.q: Why are astronauts weightless in space?

weight-calculator.formula:
Weight = mass x gravity.
Newtons: W (N) = m (kg) x g (m/s squared).
Kilogram-force: kgf = W / 9.80665.
Pound-force: lbf = W x 0.224809.
Example: 70 kg on the Moon: 70 x 1.62 = 113.4 N.
howTo: Pick your mass unit: kilograms or pounds.
Enter your mass - the number your bathroom scale shows in kg is close enough.
Choose a planet or moon from the list, or pick Custom gravity and type any value.
Read your weight instantly in newtons, kilogram-force, and pound-force.
Compare Earth with the Moon and Jupiter to feel how gravity shapes weight.
keyFacts: Weight is a force: W = mass x gravity, measured in newtons (N), not kilograms.
Earth's average surface gravity is 9.807 m/s squared; the Moon's is 1.62; Jupiter's is 24.79.
Your mass is identical on every planet. A 70 kg person is 70 kg on the Moon too - but weighs only about 113 N there.
Kilogram-force (kgf) is the old unit bathroom scales use: 1 kgf = 9.80665 N. On Earth, kgf and kg look the same.
Pound-force (lbf) is the imperial unit of force: 1 lbf = 4.44822 N.
The Sun's surface gravity is about 274 m/s squared - roughly 28 times Earth's. Do not try this at home.

limitations: Uses average surface gravity; real gravity varies slightly with altitude and location.
The listed planets are gas or ice giants - you could not actually stand on their surfaces.
Weight in kilogram-force is a force unit, not a mass - scales blur this distinction on Earth.
This is an educational estimate, not lab-grade measurement.

weight-calculator.quickAnswer: Weight = mass x gravity. A 70 kg person weighs about 686 N on Earth (70.0 kgf / 154.3 lbf), about 113 N on the Moon, and about 1,736 N on Jupiter. Your mass never changes - only the pull of gravity does. Pick a planet above and this tool shows your weight in newtons, kilogram-force, and pound-force instantly.

weight-calculator.workedExample:
Mass 70 kg, on the Moon (g = 1.62 m/s squared):
1. Weight in newtons: 70 x 1.62 = 113.4 N.
2. Kilogram-force: 113.4 / 9.80665 = 11.56 kgf.
3. Pound-force: 113.4 x 0.224809 = 25.49 lbf.
For comparison on Earth: 70 x 9.807 = 686.49 N = 70.00 kgf = 154.33 lbf.
Same mass, very different weight - gravity does all the work.

whitespace-remover.formula:
Options apply in this order:

1. Remove ALL whitespace: text with every \s removed -> done.
2. Remove tabs: each tab becomes one space.
3. Remove line breaks: every run of line breaks becomes one space.
4. Collapse multiple spaces: runs of 2+ spaces become one space.
5. Trim each line: leading and trailing spaces removed per line.
6. Remove empty lines: blank lines dropped.

characters removed = input length - output length

  2. trim lines: 'hello world\n\nfoo' (16 chars)
  3. remove empty: 'hello world\nfoo' (15 chars)

faqs.a: Wind chill describes how cold the air feels on exposed skin when wind strips away the thin layer of warm air your body maintains. At 0°C with a 20 km/h wind, the air feels like minus 5.2°C. It is a feels-like temperature, not an actual temperature — your thermometer still reads 0°C.
faqs.q: What is wind chill exactly?

faqs.a: The official formula (used by weather services in the US, Canada, and the UK) was developed from experiments on human volunteers in cold wind tunnels. It models heat loss from exposed skin. It is well validated inside its range: at or below 10°C with wind above 4.8 km/h. Outside that range it is meaningless.
faqs.q: Is the wind chill formula accurate?

faqs.a: Wind chill cannot go above the actual air temperature — if it feels warmer than the thermometer, that is humidity or sunshine, not wind chill. Also, wind chill applies to exposed skin, so it does not tell you how fast a car radiator or a water pipe will cool.
faqs.q: Can wind chill be warmer than the air temperature?

faqs.a: Cover exposed skin: balaclava or scarf, insulated gloves, and windproof outer layers. The risk badge on this page follows Environment Canada guidance: below minus 28°C, exposed skin can freeze within 30 minutes; below minus 40°C, within 10 minutes. Keep trips short and check on other people.
faqs.q: How do I stay safe when wind chill is very low?

faqs.a: No. Wind chill is only defined for cold conditions. For hot weather, weather services use the heat index, which combines temperature and humidity to estimate how hot it feels. JaurTools plans a heat index calculator as a companion tool.
faqs.q: Is there a summer version of wind chill?

faqs.a: Because your body heats a thin boundary layer of air next to your skin, and wind constantly replaces it with cold air. The faster the wind, the faster heat is carried away, so your skin cools toward the wind chill value rather than the still-air temperature.
faqs.q: Why does wind make cold feel colder?

T = air temperature in °C, V = wind speed in km/h.
Valid only when T ≤ 10°C and V ≥ 4.8 km/h.

localTime(Z) = Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { timeZone: Z, hour, minute, second })

xirr-calculator.formula:
XNPV(r) = sum of CF_i / (1 + r)^((d_i - d_0) / 365).
XIRR is the rate r where XNPV(r) = 0.
Solved here with Newton-Raphson iteration from a 10% starting guess.
Example: -10,000 on 2024-01-01, +11,000 on 2025-01-01 -> r ~ 9.97%.

faqs.a: A z-score measures how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean: z = (x − μ) / σ. A z of 0 means exactly average; +2 means two standard deviations above the mean.

faqs.a: The percentile is Φ(z) × 100 — the percentage of a normal distribution at or below your value. A z of 1.5 gives the 93.32nd percentile: about 93.3% of values fall below.

z-score-calculator.formula:
z = (x − μ) / σ

x = your value, μ = mean, σ = standard deviation

Percentile = Φ(z) × 100, where Φ is the standard normal CDF:
Φ(z) = (1 / √(2π)) ∫₋∞ᵗ e^(−t²/2) dt

The tool evaluates Φ with a high-precision rational approximation
(error below 7.5 × 10⁻⁸), so no table lookup is needed.

Enter the mean μ of the distribution it comes from.

zalgo-text-generator.formula:

for each character c in input:

  if c is whitespace: continue
  if above on:  append `level` random marks from the 52-char UP set (U+0300-U+036F)
  if through on: append `level` random marks from the 15-char MID set
  if below on:  append `level` random marks from the 40-char DOWN set
marks added = letters x level x (directions on)

faqs.a: A bond that pays no periodic interest. You buy it below face value and receive the full face value at maturity. The difference is your return. US Treasury STRIPS and many government savings bonds work this way.
faqs.q: What is a zero-coupon bond?

faqs.a: Because there are no coupons to cushion the blow, zero-coupon bonds are the most interest-rate-sensitive bonds. When market yields rise, their prices fall hard; when yields fall, they rise hard. Longer maturities amplify the effect.
faqs.q: Why are zero prices so sensitive to rates?

faqs.a: Yield to maturity is the annualised return you earn if you buy at the market price and hold to maturity. Solve: yield = (face value / price)^(1/years) - 1. This calculator's yield mode does it for you.
faqs.q: What is yield to maturity?

faqs.a: Often yes for taxes: many countries tax the imputed annual interest on zero-coupon bonds even though you receive no cash until maturity (phantom income). Check your local tax rules before buying - the tax treatment can surprise first-time buyers.
faqs.q: Are zeros taxed before maturity?

faqs.a: Holding to maturity locks in the yield you calculated. Selling early exposes you to market price swings: if rates rose, you get less than the fair hold-to-maturity value. Zeros suit investors with a known future cash need, like tuition in 10 years.
faqs.q: Should I hold to maturity or trade?

faqs.a: Reinvestment risk - the risk that coupon payments must be reinvested at lower rates - disappears, because there are no coupons. That makes zeros the purest play on a future interest rate: what you see is what you get if you hold to maturity.
faqs.q: Do zeros have reinvestment risk?

zero-coupon-bond-calculator.formula:
Price = face value / (1 + yield)^years.
Yield = (face value / price)^(1 / years) - 1.
Discount = face value - price.
Example: 1,000 / 1.05^10 = 613.91; yield from 613.91 = 5.00%.

faqs.a: Compression ratio = (1 − packed size ÷ original size) × 100. Text files often compress 60–80%; already-compressed formats like JPEG, MP4, and PNG barely shrink, so a low ratio on those is normal, not a problem.

faqs.a: Yes. The central directory stores each entry's original size, packed size, compression method, and name — everything this tool shows. Filenames are decoded as UTF-8, which covers virtually all modern archives.

faqs.a: A valid format means the code matches the country's pattern — it does not prove the code exists or that mail will reach it. A six-digit Indian PIN like 999999 matches the pattern but may not be a real PIN. For existence checks, use the country's postal service lookup.
faqs.q: Does valid mean the code really exists?

faqs.a: The UAE has never operated a public postal-code system; mail is delivered to PO boxes instead. So any 'UAE postal code' you see in a form is either the PO box number or made up. This tool tells you that directly instead of pretending to validate it.
faqs.q: Why does the UAE show as not used?

faqs.a: Yes — the US ZIP+4 format (five digits, hyphen, four digits, like 90210-1234) is accepted alongside the plain five-digit ZIP. Both are official US formats.
faqs.q: Are US ZIP+4 codes accepted?

faqs.a: No. British postcodes mix letters and digits (for example, SW1A 1AA), so the check is case-insensitive and allows the optional space. Typing sw1a1aa is just as valid as SW1A 1AA.
faqs.q: Do UK postcodes have to be uppercase?

faqs.a: Yes. Indian PIN codes are six digits and the first digit is never 0 — it runs 1–9 by postal region. Codes like 012345 are rejected by this tool, matching India Post's own numbering.
faqs.q: Why do Indian PIN codes reject a leading zero?

faqs.a: Correct. Japan's 7-digit codes are written with a hyphen after the third digit (100-0001), and the hyphen is required here. Brazil accepts the hyphen as optional (01310100 and 01310-100 both pass).
faqs.q: Is the hyphen required in Japanese codes?

UK: ^[A-Z]{1,2}[0-9][A-Z0-9]?\s?[0-9][A-Z]{2}$  (case-insensitive)
Japan: ^\d{3}-\d{4}$  (hyphen required)

benefits: Translate abstract zoom numbers into real-world map scales.
Essential for cartographers, GIS users, and print map design.
Ground-resolution numbers help you pick the right zoom for detail work.
Compare how scale changes with latitude and screen DPI.

faqs.a: In the Web Mercator projection used by Google Maps, OpenStreetMap, and most web maps, the world is 256 pixels wide at zoom 0 and doubles with each zoom level. Each integer zoom step halves the ground distance per pixel, so zoom 10 shows half the detail width of zoom 9 but four times the map area detail per tile.
faqs.q: What does a zoom level actually mean?

faqs.a: Ground resolution = 156543.03392 × cos(latitude) ÷ 2^zoom metres per pixel. At the equator (latitude 0), cos = 1, so zoom 10 gives 156543.03392 ÷ 1024 = 152.87 m/px. Multiply by pixels-per-metre on your screen (DPI ÷ 0.0254) to get the scale denominator.
faqs.q: How is ground resolution calculated?

faqs.a: Because Web Mercator stretches the world toward the poles, one screen pixel covers less ground as latitude increases — multiplied by cos(latitude). At 60° latitude, cos = 0.5, so everything is at half the equatorial ground resolution for the same zoom.
faqs.q: Why does latitude change the scale?

faqs.a: Scale 1:N means 1 unit on the map represents N units on the ground. A larger N means a smaller scale (less detail, more area). Zoom 10 at 96 DPI is about 1:578,000 — a regional map. Zoom 15 is about 1:18,000 — street level.
faqs.q: What does 1:578,000 mean?

faqs.a: No — only if the DPI matches. A 96 DPI desktop monitor, a 150 DPI laptop, and a 300 DPI printout all show the same zoom level at different physical scales. That is why this calculator asks for your screen DPI before computing the scale.
faqs.q: Is the scale the same on every screen?

faqs.a: Web maps max out around zoom 19–22 depending on the provider (Google Maps goes to about 22 in some areas). Beyond that, tiles are simply magnified, not more detailed. This calculator accepts 0–22.
faqs.q: What is the maximum zoom level?

zoom-level-to-map-scale-calculator.formula:
Ground resolution = 156543.03392 × cos(latitude) / 2^zoom  (metres per pixel)
Map scale denominator N = ground resolution × (DPI / 0.0254)
Scale is written 1:N. 1 inch = 0.0254 m exactly.
howTo: Drag the zoom slider to the level you want to convert (0–22).
Enter the latitude of the area — scale shrinks toward the poles.
Pick your screen DPI (96 is the common desktop default).
Read the map scale, ground resolution, and ground distance per screen centimetre.
keyFacts: Web Mercator maps double in detail with each integer zoom level.
At the equator, zoom 0 = 156,543 metres per pixel.
Zoom 10 at the equator and 96 DPI is about 1:578,000.
Ground resolution shrinks by cos(latitude) toward the poles.

faqs.q: How does the background color work?
faqs.a: The tool draws a full-page colored rectangle behind your page content, then places your original page on top. Text and images are untouched — they just sit on a colored sheet now.

faqs.q: Why can I not see the color on some pages?
faqs.a: If a page is a full-page photo or scan, that image covers the color completely. The background shows wherever the page itself is blank or transparent.

faqs.q: What is a good opacity for reading?
faqs.a: For reading tints, 100% opacity with a light color (like warm paper #fef3c7) works best. Lower opacities are for subtle effects over existing designs.

faqs.q: Can I use my brand exact color?
faqs.a: Yes — type the hex code (e.g. #1e3a8a) into the color field for a precise match.

faqs.q: Will it print the background?
faqs.a: Yes, the color is part of the PDF. Note that PDF viewers have a 'print backgrounds' setting, and full-page color uses more ink.

faqs.q: Does it work in dark mode?
faqs.a: The preview adapts to your theme. For a dark-reading effect, pick a dark color like #1e293b — light text stays readable on top.

faqs.q: Is this the same as PDF to Text?
faqs.a: Similar extraction, different output: PDF to Text gives plain text, while this produces structured HTML with paragraphs, page sections, and styling — ready for the web.

faqs.q: Will the HTML look like my PDF?
faqs.a: No — and that is intentional. You get clean, readable, semantic content you can restyle, not a pixel-perfect replica. For visual fidelity, convert pages to images instead.

faqs.q: What about tables and images?
faqs.a: Tables come through as plain text lines (structure is lost), and images are skipped. Complex layouts need manual cleanup after conversion.

faqs.q: Why is my scanned PDF empty?
faqs.a: Scans are pictures of text with no embedded characters. This tool extracts embedded text only; scanned documents need OCR software first.

faqs.q: Can I edit the HTML afterwards?
faqs.a: Absolutely — it's standard HTML with inline CSS. Open it in any editor, change the styles, or paste sections into your website.

faqs.q: Does it handle Arabic or Hindi text?
faqs.a: Yes. Extracted Unicode text is preserved, and Arabic documents automatically get right-to-left direction in the output.
